Did Ovid write any iambs? Not in his surviving verse--most of it is written in dactyls, with a few spondees thrown in for spice.

But in English translation, however:

Here's a passage from 1567, written by Arthur Golding in iambic heptameter, which may have inspired the Bard of Avon:

Within the towne (of whose huge walles so monstrous high and thicke
The fame is given Semyramis for making them of bricke)
Dwelt hard together two yong folke in houses joynde so nere
That under all one roofe well nie both twaine conveyed were.
The name of him was Pyramus, and Thisbe calde was she.
So faire a man in all the East was none alive as he,
Nor nere a woman, maide nor wife in beautie like to hir.

By comparison, here's a version published in 1717 by Samuel Garth, bringing together work "by the most eminent hands," a veritable who's who of the time, including Johnnie Dryden, Alec Pope, and Billy Congreve:

In Babylon, where first her Queen, for State
Rais'd Walls of Brick magnificently great,
Liv'd Pyramus, and Thisbe, lovely Pair!
He found no Eastern Youth his Equal there,
And she beyond the fairest Nymph was fair.

(not sure whose hands were involved.)

Thank you, Wikisource!

I'm always pleased to see reference to one of my favorite places on the planet, and one I have had the privilege to have visited and done research on: the deep-sea hydrothermal vents. A truly magical and wondrous thing on our world and one that was completely unknown until 1977, when research largely conducted by marine geologists and geophysicists from Oregon State University pointed to their existence, finally confirmed by the first visit to the vents in the Alvin. There were no biologists on this research cruise, since the assumption was that the environment around the vents would be highly toxic and barren of life. 

Little did they know 

The first message we received was "Send biologists!" (I was working in the Marine Geology Department at the OSU School of Oceanography at the time.) 

It was two years before a biological expedition was made. And its was 15 years before I went there myself. A research cruise I will never forget.

@Nancy (really to @SP)
A few hours ago, I made a comment about the "weirdness" of current celebs' names. I should explain myself further:

Our English language tradition of naming follows a system taken from ancient Rome (which they probably got from the Etruscans), in which is a closed set of first names--about a dozen for men, a few more for women--followed by a surname which is passed down from generation to generation. (This is not the original Indo-European system, which gave us Vladi-mir, Sieg-fried, and even Al-fred.)  The operative words here are "closed set." I, myself, am part of that set.

On the other hand, many communities--in particular the African-American community, but there are many others--have traditions in which new names are constantly being coined or modified. In other words, an "open set."Of course, once in a while you come across some pretty silly examples--O father of Lavoris, what wert thou thinking?--but, in general, I find it a genuinely admirable, beautiful practice.

And, of course, as our American society becomes less WASP-centered, traditional names from other cultures will become part of the set.
